topic.title: the driver and the bai
topic.claim: In Mumbai homes the driver, working a few hours a day, is paid more than the bai who works all day across homes, because a man's work is priced as a job and a woman's as housework.
topic.moment: You compare what your driver and your bai get: a month's salary as Diwali bonus for both, and his is bigger.

turn.believed: Household staff are paid fairly by the work.
turn.actually: They're paid by gender: driving is a job, housework starts at a discount.

topic.because: Housework is what women in the family did for free, so a woman doing it for pay starts at a discount, while driving is treated as a man's skilled job.
topic.payoff: With no national law, the household is her only labour law: every salary day it sets what women's work is worth, and the kids learn the rate.
topic.send_to: the friend in Mumbai who negotiates with the bai and never with the driver

sources.excerpt: 2.79 crore domestic & household workers have registered on e-shram portal out of which 2.67 crore are women.

sources.fact: India has no national law for domestic workers: since 1959, government and private member bills sought to fix their wages and give them social security, but none resulted in a national law (Scroll, 9 April 2026).
sources.excerpt: Since 1959, government and private member bills have sought to regulate domestic work by fixing wages and bringing about registration and social security but none have resulted in a national law.

cover.headline: In your Mumbai home, the one who works hardest gets paid least.
cover.sub: It's the bai, not the driver.

paragraphs: In your Mumbai home, the one who works hardest gets paid least.
It's the bai, not the driver.
Look at your own building.
Your driver drops you to office, waits in the car, and brings you home.
Your bai cooks, sweeps and washes across three or four homes, seven days a week.
Yet he earns more.
And at Diwali, when you give both a month's salary as a bonus, his bonus is bigger too.
It isn't the work. It's who does it.
Driving is a man's job, so you pay it like one.
Cooking and cleaning are what your mother did for nothing. So when a woman does them for money, the price starts low.
Listen to how you talk about it.
Nobody says "just driving". Everyone says "just jhadu-pocha".
And when he takes leave, you book an Uber.
When she takes leave, the whole house stops.
This isn't just your building.
2.79 crore Indians have signed up with the labour ministry as domestic workers.
Almost all of them are women.
So if you pay her less, nobody will stop you.
India has no national law for domestic workers. Nothing fixes her pay or gives her social security.
For the woman in your kitchen, the only labour law is you.
Every salary day, your house decides what a woman's work is worth.
And your kids are watching the rate.

c2.correct: India has no dedicated national law for domestic workers; the Centre has opposed creating one, choosing instead to rely on the four general labour codes (notified Nov 2025) whose applicability to domestic workers is itself unclear in three of the four codes.

sources.quote: since 1959, government and private member bills have sought to regulate domestic work by fixing wages and bringing about registration and social security but none have resulted in a national law... there being no clarity on inclusion of domestic workers in three of the four codes, barring the Code on Social Security, 2020.
The Central Government has not enacted any separate law to protect the interest of domestic workers... Homes...are not recognised as workplaces for domestic and home-based workers in the labour code.

c3.correct: The Code on Wages, 2019 only empowers governments to fix minimum wages; it provides no formula or actual fixed rate for domestic workers, and no state has successfully implemented one.

sources.quote: The Code on Wages, 2019 empowers both Central and State Governments...to fix, review and revise the minimum rates of wages.

the new code does not provide a formula for the calculation of this minimum wage for domestic and home-based workers... 19 of 36 states added domestic workers to minimum wage schedules, but no states have so far successfully implemented this.

c4.correct: Only the Code on Social Security, 2020 even mentions domestic workers, and it does so by pointing to voluntary, optional general welfare schemes (e.g. e-Shram-linked schemes) with no clarity on actual implementation, not a guaranteed PF or insurance entitlement.

sources.quote: Only the Code on Social Security explicitly mentions domestic workers... the report 'relies on general welfare schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana' without clarity on actual implementation.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 'classifies domestic and home-based workers as wage workers.' Yet implementation remains weak—schemes are voluntary and optional rather than mandatory.

c5.correct: The 2.8 crore figure is from March 2023; the number has since risen to about 2.89 crore (28.9 million) as of March 2025 and is likely somewhat higher by the Nov 2026 go-live, but the scale ('about 2.8 crore') is still roughly right.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: Within one Mumbai household a full-time driver (roughly ₹18,000–30,000/month, averaging about ₹19,000) is paid more per home than a part-time bai (about ₹3,500–9,000/home), so the per-household gap the post describes is real. But the price difference is set substantially by labour structure, not only gender: a driver is exclusive to one employer for the whole day (full opportunity cost, licence, legal liability on the road), while cooking-cleaning is divisible, so the bai sells fractions of her day to 3–4 homes and each home pays only for its slice — across all her homes her aggregate earnings often match or beat a single driver's. The gendered devaluation of care work the post reads into this is a documented and defensible interpretation layered on top of that structural mechanism, not a falsifiable factual claim.

sources.quote: The average salary for a driver is ₹18,957 per month in Mumbai, Maharashtra.
Part-time maids working 1–4 hours daily earn ₹3,500 to ₹7,000 per month, while full-time maids working 8 hours earn ₹10,000 to ₹14,000.
City-wise rates for maids, cooks, nannies & drivers show full-time drivers in metros like Mumbai earning ₹18,000–₹30,000, above typical part-time maid wages.

alt_texts: In your Mumbai home, the one who works hardest gets paid least. It's the bai, not the driver.
Look at your own building. Your driver drops you to office, waits in the car, and brings you home. Your bai cooks, sweeps and washes across three or four homes, seven days a week.
Yet he earns more. And at Diwali, when you give both a month's salary as a bonus, his bonus is bigger too.

It isn't the work. It's who does it. Driving is a man's job, so you pay it like one. Cooking and cleaning are what your mother did for nothing. So when a woman does them for money, the price starts low.
Listen to how you talk about it. Nobody says "just driving". Everyone says "just jhadu-pocha".
And when he takes leave, you book an Uber. When she takes leave, the whole house stops.
This isn't just your building. 2.79 crore Indians have signed up with the labour ministry as domestic workers. Almost all of them are women.

So if you pay her less, nobody will stop you. India has no national law for domestic workers. Nothing fixes her pay or gives her social security. For the woman in your kitchen, the only labour law is you.
Every salary day, your house decides what a woman's work is worth. And your kids are watching the rate.

history.point: The maid works harder than the driver but gets paid and valued less because of old-fashioned ideas about which work 'counts' as a job.
history.reason: Because driving is treated as a man's real job you pay for, while cooking and cleaning is seen as unpaid 'mother's work', so its price starts low even when done for money.
ideas: the maid is overworked and underpaid compared to the driver because of gender bias in how household labour is valued

history.point: In most Indian homes, the woman who cooks and cleans (the bai) works harder than the male driver but gets paid less and respected less, purely because of her gender.
history.reason: Because society already labels driving as a man's job worth paying for, while cooking and cleaning are seen as what mothers did for free, so the price for a woman doing that work starts low.

lost.why: had to re-read the two crore figures and wasn't told which 'government register' this is, so it felt like a new source dropped in without introduction

ideas: Household pay and respect for domestic work is gendered, not based on effort — and there's no law to fix it since it's left entirely to the employer's conscience

history.point: In most Indian homes, the woman who cooks and cleans works harder than the driver but gets paid and treated as worth less, simply because it's seen as a woman's job.
history.reason: Because driving is seen as a man's job and valued like one, while cooking and cleaning is what mothers did for free, so when a woman is paid for it, the price starts low.
ideas: Domestic women workers are paid and valued less than drivers purely because of gender, not effort, and this goes unchecked because no law protects them

c2.correct: India has no dedicated national law for domestic workers; the Centre has opposed creating one, choosing instead to rely on the four general labour codes (notified Nov 2025) whose applicability to domestic workers is itself unclear in three of the four codes.

c3.correct: The Code on Wages, 2019 only empowers governments to fix minimum wages; it provides no formula or actual fixed rate for domestic workers, and no state has successfully implemented one.

the new code does not provide a formula for the calculation of this minimum wage for domestic and home-based workers... 19 of 36 states added domestic workers to minimum wage schedules, but no states have so far successfully implemented this.

c4.correct: Only the Code on Social Security, 2020 even mentions domestic workers, and it does so by pointing to voluntary, optional general welfare schemes (e.g. e-Shram-linked schemes) with no clarity on actual implementation, not a guaranteed PF or insurance entitlement.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: Within one Mumbai household a full-time driver (roughly ₹18,000–30,000/month, averaging about ₹19,000) is paid more per home than a part-time bai (about ₹3,500–9,000/home), so the per-household gap the post describes is real. But the price difference is set substantially by labour structure, not only gender: a driver is exclusive to one employer for the whole day (full opportunity cost, licence, legal liability on the road), while cooking-cleaning is divisible, so the bai sells fractions of her day to 3–4 homes and each home pays only for its slice — across all her homes her aggregate earnings often match or beat a single driver's. The gendered devaluation of care work the post reads into this is a documented and defensible interpretation layered on top of that structural mechanism, not a falsifiable factual claim.

sources.quote: The average salary for a driver is ₹18,957 per month in Mumbai, Maharashtra.
Part-time maids working 1–4 hours daily earn ₹3,500 to ₹7,000 per month, while full-time maids working 8 hours earn ₹10,000 to ₹14,000.
City-wise rates for maids, cooks, nannies & drivers show full-time drivers in metros like Mumbai earning ₹18,000–₹30,000, above typical part-time maid wages.
